sections.heading: Scarcity and opportunity cost in Principles of Economics I
paragraphs: Scarcity and opportunity cost is studied here as a specific part of Principles of Economics I. Begin by defining the term precisely and identifying the problem it helps explain or solve. Keep the scope narrow: related ideas may interact with it, but they are not interchangeable.

Economics studies choices under scarcity and how incentives shape allocation. Separate a movement along a curve, caused by a change in a variable already on an axis, from a shift of the entire curve caused by another determinant. State whether a claim is positive (testable) or normative (value-based).

For this topic, distinguish the central principle from its assumptions. Ask: what is given, what must be inferred or calculated, what evidence would support the conclusion, and in what circumstances would the conclusion no longer hold? At introductory level, establish accurate definitions first, then explain the relationship between concepts and practise a worked example. Be able to explain the idea in your own words rather than memorising a phrase.

sections.heading: Worked application
paragraphs: If demand rises while supply is unchanged, the demand curve shifts right. At the old price there is excess demand, which creates upward pressure on price. The new equilibrium generally has a higher price and higher quantity, provided the usual upward-sloping supply and downward-sloping demand assumptions hold.

examples.title: Worked application: Demand and supply
steps: Demand describes quantities consumers are willing and able to buy at different prices over a period, holding other determinants constant. Supply describes quantities producers are willing and able to offer. A change in the good’s own price produces movement along a curve; changes in income, tastes, input costs, technology, or expectations may shift a curve.

practiceQuestions.prompt: If consumer income rises and the good is normal, what is the usual effect on demand?
options: The supply curve must shift left
There is only movement along the demand curve caused by the good’s price
practiceQuestions.explanation: For a normal good, higher income tends to increase demand at each price, shifting the demand curve right.

examples.title: Worked application: Elasticity basics
steps: Price elasticity of demand is percentage change in quantity demanded divided by percentage change in price. Its sign is usually negative under the conventional demand relationship, though textbooks often discuss the absolute magnitude. Elasticity differs from slope because it uses percentage changes and depends on the point on the curve.

Write a conclusion that answers the question directly and notes one relevant limitation.

practiceQuestions.prompt: If quantity demanded changes by −10% when price rises by 5%, what is the price elasticity of demand?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Elasticity is −10%/5%=−2; the absolute value is 2, indicating elastic demand over that change.
